strengths: The paper offers a clear conceptual framing of 'functional entanglement' as a failure mode of free-form LLM-driven NAS, and proposes a principled decomposition (select factor -> emit directive -> factor-scoped edit) that is backbone-agnostic and easy to integrate into existing evolutionary search loops.

The ablation in Table 2 is informative: it separates ASR (scope selection) from RC+SAR (within-scope refinement) under two different LLM editors (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-Plus), and consistently shows that scope selection is the larger contributor. This is a useful, transferable insight for the LLM-NAS community.

The engineering design (region tags + syntax/interface/shape feasibility checks that reject invalid proposals before evaluation) is practical and the paper is careful about budget accounting (proposed vs. evaluated candidates), which is a genuine methodological detail often glossed over in LLM-NAS work.

The paper reports per-task CLRS results, cross-task transfer, reliability curves (entanglement rate, cumulative valid rate), and multi-seed dynamics in the appendix, which is more evidence than many LLM-NAS papers provide.
weaknesses: The headline 28.1x sample-efficiency claim is not supported by a fair comparison. It is computed as 1600/57, comparing SPARK's best-so-far on a single DFS run against EvoPrompting's 1600-evaluation setting, which spans multi-task evolution. The paper itself acknowledges that EP 'performs evolution across multiple tasks' while SPARK evolves only on DFS, so this ratio conflates different budgets and protocols and cannot substantiate the abstract/abstract-introduction claim.

A critical control is missing: there is no ablation isolating the feasibility pipeline (syntax/interface/shape checks) without factor scoping. Since the feasibility pipeline is factor-invariant (constraint C) and rejects invalid candidates, it is plausible that much of the gain comes from filtering broken proposals rather than from factor isolation. Without this control, the attribution of gains to 'reducing entanglement' is not established.

The reported task counts are inconsistent and appear cherry-picked. The Abstract/Introduction/Table 1 discuss '10 CLRS tasks'; the Conclusion states 'improves over the reference on 12/18 tasks and outperforms EvoPrompting on 10/18'; Table A.1 lists 30 tasks. Main-text Table 1 shows SPARK best on all listed tasks, while Table A.1 shows large regressions (BFS 99.7 -> 70.6; FW 48.5 -> 32.9; MCO 91.7 -> 87.3; KMP 19.5 -> 14.9) and losses vs. EP on several tasks. This contradicts the 'Across all listed tasks, SPARK achieves the best OOD accuracy' framing and undermines trust in the reported numbers.

The entanglement-rate metric (Fig. 2b) is largely tautological: SPARK explicitly forbids edits outside the selected region, so its lower entanglement rate is guaranteed by construction rather than being evidence of a causal mechanism linking entanglement to search performance. The accompanying feasibility model (p_v^k) is asserted, not measured.

Main results appear to come from a single seed with no error bars or significance tests (Table 1, Table 2). The 5-seed analysis in the appendix only covers dynamics (Fig. A.1), not the main comparison, so the stability of the reported effect sizes (e.g., 83.74 vs. 65.28 ASR-only) is unknown. The superadditive ASR+RC+SAR gain over both partial variants is also unexplained.

Reproducibility is limited: prompts, region-tag specification, feasibility implementation details, and the exact search configuration are not provided in the main text; the LLM is an API endpoint (DeepSeek-R1-0528) with temperature 0.7 and no seed control reported. Key claims (e.g., the 28.1x figure) therefore cannot be independently verified from the manuscript alone.

The MACs discussion is conceptually confused. The paper states MACs can be 'viewed as the CLRS reference compute plus a small, fixed overhead introduced by the SPARK editing interface,' but MACs measure the evaluated architecture, not the editing process; the editing interface does not enter MACs. This framing conflates search cost with model capacity.

Reference handling raises integrity concerns: several references are irrelevant to the topic (steel-sheet defect detection, person re-identification, image-goal navigation, homography estimation, video captioning, cloud removal) and are cited in the appendix architecture-evolution discussion; dates/keys are mismatched (e.g., 'Chen et al. (2019)' citing a 2023 paper; 'Fu et al. (2023a) arXiv:1909.03258, 2019'; 'Qi et al. 2026, arXiv:2603.05869'). This looks like citation padding and weakens confidence in the manuscript's care and integrity.

Presentation is overwrought: pervasive bolding, scare-quoted jargon ('where-then-how', 'Function-factor Tokens', 'Searching: Function->Patch'), and a figure containing non-English characters. The dense terminology obscures rather than clarifies the relatively simple underlying mechanism (region-restricted diff + feasibility filter).

strengths: The core idea of restricting each LLM edit to a single explicit functional factor (OPERATOR vs ACTION), enforced with region tags plus syntax/interface/shape feasibility checks, is an intuitive and reasonably well-specified mechanism for making code-level LLM edits more controllable and executable.

The paper makes a genuine attempt to evaluate the search process itself rather than only final accuracy, reporting best-so-far progress, an entanglement rate, and a cumulative valid-rate curve (Fig. 2), and it includes an ablation that separates the scope-routing (ASR) component from the refinement (RC+SAR) component across two LLM editors.

The feasibility pipeline and the operationalization of factor-local edits (normalized line-based diff mapped to tagged regions, with byte-identity checks on the frozen region) are described concretely enough to be reimplemented, and the reliance on a frozen training/evaluation harness is a reasonable control for isolating architecture effects.
The DFS result (83.74% OOD) and several graph-reasoning gains (CC, TS) are substantial and, if reproduced, would be a useful signal that locality-constrained editing helps on such tasks.
weaknesses: The headline 28.1x "sample-efficient architecture evolution speedup" is not a controlled efficiency comparison: it is computed as 1600/57, i.e., the ratio between EvoPrompting's much larger evaluation budget and SPARK's own 57 evaluated candidates. Nothing demonstrates that SPARK reaches comparable quality with fewer evaluations under a matched budget; the number simply reflects that SPARK was run with a 100-attempt budget while EvoPrompting was run with 1600. This central quantitative claim is therefore an artifact of protocol mismatch.

The comparison protocol is confounded. The paper states it performs evolution only on DFS and then transfers the best architecture to the other 9 tasks, while "EvoPrompting performs evolution across multiple tasks." Comparing SPARK's transfer performance against per-task evolved baselines is not an apples-to-apples test, and the reported "83.92% mean OOD accuracy across 10 tasks" is a transfer result, not evidence about the search operator. The NAS contribution is thus effectively demonstrated on a single task (DFS).

The narrative overstates the results relative to the authors' own data. Section 4.2 claims SPARK "achieves the best OOD accuracy, consistently outperforming the CLRS reference architecture as well as strong LLM-evolution baselines," yet Table A.1 and the conclusion indicate improvements over the reference on only 12/18 tasks and over EvoPrompting on 10/18, with large regressions (BFS 99.7 -> 70.6, FW 48.5 -> 32.9, MCO 91.7 -> 87.3, MKr 89.8 -> 86.2). The abstract/introduction foreground DFS and a few favorable tasks, so the headline numbers are selective.

There is an unexplained, potentially decisive inconsistency between the main text and the appendix. The main claim is 83.74% best-so-far OOD on DFS, but Appendix Fig. A.1a plots "Best-so-far OOD accuracy" for SPARK over 5 seeds with a y-axis that tops out around 0.25 (25%), never approaching 83.74%. The appendix caption describes the same quantity, and no reconciliation or metric clarification is given. This directly undermines confidence in the reported search-progress results and in reproducibility.

Novelty is limited and the framing inflates it. Stripped of terminology, SPARK is (i) annotating code with region tags, (ii) asking an LLM to pick one region and edit only there, and (iii) rejecting proposals that violate the region/interface/shape constraints. "Functional entanglement" is a rebranding of the observation that a free-form edit can touch multiple code regions, and locality-constrained/grammar-or-AST-constrained editing plus validity filtering are well-established. "Structured Progressive Knowledge Activation" overstates the mechanism relative to what is actually implemented.

Evidence for the proposed causal mechanism is weak. The measured entanglement rate differs only marginally between SPARK and OpenEvolve (roughly 0.45 vs 0.50 in Fig. 2b), which is a thin basis for the strong claims about entanglement being the bottleneck. The per-scope feasibility model (p_v^k) is asserted as intuition without being tested.

The main comparison table provides no error bars or significance testing and appears to be from a single run per method, while multi-seed results are relegated to the appendix. Given the apparent high variance (e.g., the Ours-1it variant scores 45.60 on DFS, below the 46.78 CLRS reference, and 73.04 on AP, below the reference), the reported single-run best numbers cannot be distinguished from run-to-run noise.

The baseline numbers are not credible as stated. The authors state that OpenEvolve and FunSearch "do not explicitly report results on CLRS," so their numbers were produced by re-running released code inside the authors' own pipeline with a 100-attempt budget. OE scoring 32.54 on DFS (far below the 46.78 reference) and other baselines being uniformly weak is not reconciled with the original papers, and re-running baselines under a bespoke 100-attempt budget and a custom harness may not faithfully represent those methods, biasing comparisons in SPARK's favor.

Reproducibility is under-supported: no code or artifact release is indicated, the LLM editor is an API-only black box (DeepSeek-R1-0528), prompts are only referenced by name (RoutePrompt/DirectivePrompt/EditPrompt) without content, and key details (number of runs behind Table 1, seeds, cascade thresholds) are either missing or pushed to a supplementary that is not summarized quantitatively.

Presentation and scholarly hygiene are poor. The reference list contains numerous off-topic citations with no relation to NAS or LLM-driven search (e.g., steel-sheet defect recognition, homography estimation, cloud removal, video captioning, image-goal navigation), suggesting citation padding, and there are multiple bibliographic errors and mismatches (e.g., a key labeled "Chen et al. (2019)" with year 2023; "Dong et al. (2019)" for a 2020 paper; several "Wu et al."/"Li et al." entries with missing or misassigned authors/years; an empty "Li et al. (2025c)" entry).

The ablation design does not cleanly isolate the claimed factor. "ASR only" and "RC+SAR only" are not natural decompositions of a factor-conditioned editor (ASR without any scoped refinement is not a coherent editing operator), so the conclusion that scope localization is "more critical than refinement" is weakly supported. Table 2 also reports only single-task (DFS) results on one metric.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible and well-motivated failure mode—'functional entanglement'—in LLM-driven NAS, where free-form edits couple interacting functional decisions (OPERATOR and ACTION) and break executability or confound credit assignment.

The SPARK method is concretely specified: the ASR/RC/SAR decomposition, factor-scoped tokenization with region tags, and the factor-respecting feasibility pipeline (syntax, interface, shape/masking checks) are described with algorithms and formulas, making the mechanism reasonably clear.

The controlled ablation in Table 2 (ASR only vs. RC+SAR only vs. full SPARK, under two different LLM editors) is a useful diagnostic and shows that scope selection contributes a substantial portion of the gain.

The paper carefully distinguishes 'proposal attempts' from 'evaluated candidates' and provides reliability/progress curves (Fig. 2), which is a reasonable way to study search dynamics under a fixed attempt budget.
Testing with two LLM editors (DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen-Plus) is a good practice that partially controls for model-specific effects.
weaknesses: Selective reporting undermines the central claims. Table 1 lists only the 10 tasks where SPARK wins and states SPARK 'achieves the best OOD accuracy' across all listed tasks, but the appendix (Table A.1) shows SPARK loses badly on many other tasks (BFS 99.7→70.6, FW 48.5→32.9, MCO 91.7→87.3, KMP 19.5→14.9, MKr 89.8→86.2, NSM 78.7→77.3). The main text therefore overstates the result relative to the full evidence.

There are persistent internal inconsistencies about scope: the main text says results cover '10 CLRS tasks' (an additional 9 plus DFS), the Conclusion says 'improves over the reference on 12/18 tasks and outperforms EvoPrompting on 10/18,' and the appendix header says '30 CLRS tasks' while listing ~29. This inconsistency in a core experimental claim erodes confidence in the reported numbers.

The headline '28.1× sample-efficient speedup' rests on a single task (DFS) and is computed as 1600/57 by comparing SPARK's evaluated candidates to EvoPrompting's published 1600-evaluation budget obtained under a different setup. This is not a controlled comparison, and the abstract/Introduction present it as a general property.

The main comparison table reports single-run point estimates with no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests, even though the paper claims results are reported 'over multiple random seeds.' The abstract's quantitative claims (e.g., +15.6 points, 22.9% relative improvement) are thus not statistically supported.

The entanglement-rate metric (Fig. 2b) is close to circular: SPARK is explicitly designed to enforce factor-locality, so a lower entanglement rate is largely guaranteed by construction rather than independent evidence that entanglement causes failure.

The executability/valid-rate advantage (Fig. 2c) is partly an artifact of the feasibility filter, which rejects non-factor-local candidates before they count as evaluations while OpenEvolve has no such filter. The paper does not fully disentangle whether gains come from the factor decomposition or simply from a stronger validity filter that discards attempts (the reported ~0.5–0.6 valid rate implies roughly half of SPARK's attempts are wasted).

Generality is limited. The two-factor OPERATOR/ACTION decomposition is specific to CLRS reference-code structure (two disjoint regions), and it is unclear how SPARK would be instantiated for NAS spaces where functional factors are not cleanly separable into fixed, disjoint code regions.

The reference list raises integrity/reproducibility red flags: many citations appear irrelevant to an NAS paper (e.g., steel-surface defect detection, video captioning, homography estimation, cloud removal, person re-identification) and are attached to claims they do not support; there is a future-dated citation (Qi et al. 2026, arXiv:2603.05869); and several keys have year mismatches (e.g., 'Fu et al. (2023a)' with a 2019 preprint).

Reproducibility is weak in places: results depend on a specific proprietary API model (DeepSeek-R1-0528) accessed remotely, and the prompt templates and exact region/factor definitions are deferred to an appendix that is not fully shown, making independent replication difficult.

strengths: Identifies a plausible and practically relevant failure mode: free-form LLM code edits in NAS couple multiple implicit functional decisions ('functional entanglement'), and the paper operationalizes this as a concrete diagnostic (cross-scope diffs).

The method is coherently specified: Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2, the factorization into ASR (scope selection), RC (directive), and SAR (scoped edit), and the feasibility pipeline (syntax/interface/shape checks) are described with enough detail to be reimplemented.

Scope-control ablations (Table A.2) go beyond a simple component drop-out and include region-tag-only, random-scope, fixed-scope, and RC-removed variants, which helps isolate where the gains come from (scope selection matters more than refinement alone).
Limitations are discussed honestly, explicitly noting transfer failures (BFS, Floyd-Warshall, KMP), higher search-time LLM cost, and the manual Operator/Action factorization.
Reasonable reproducibility signals: code released, a single fixed prompt template, fixed decoding hyperparameters, and an explicit statement that search initializes from the CLRS reference program.
weaknesses: The headline claim of a '28.1x sample-efficient architecture evolution speedup' is not an apples-to-apples comparison: it divides EvoPrompting's 1600 evaluations (accumulated across multiple-task evolution, as the paper itself states) by SPARK's 57 evaluated candidates on a single task (DFS). This materially overstates the efficiency claim and is the central result in the abstract and contributions.

Budget accounting systematically favors SPARK: proposals that fail feasibility 'do not count toward the evaluation budget,' while OpenEvolve/baselines with lower valid rates are penalized. Comparing evaluated-candidate counts across methods with different valid rates (and without normalizing by proposal attempts, LLM calls, or wall-clock) makes the efficiency comparison misleading; the paper's own Fig. 2 shows SPARK valid rate ~0.5-0.6 vs ~0.25-0.3 for OpenEvolve.

Main results appear to rest on single runs. Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, and Table A.2 report no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests, even though LLM-driven evolutionary search is highly stochastic and the paper elsewhere claims 'results over multiple random seeds.' Claimed differences (e.g., 83.92 vs 80.89 mean OOD, or Table 3's +36.96 pp) are not demonstrated to be statistically reliable.

The entanglement metric (Fig. 2b) is partly circular: SPARK enforces factor-local edits via region tags and feasibility rejection, so a lower entanglement rate is expected by construction and does not independently evidence improved search. The valid-rate curve (Fig. 2c) is more informative but is not separated from the constraint mechanism.

Non-CLRS comparisons are not well controlled. EoH/FunSearch use 400 candidates while OpenEvolve/Ours use 100; CartPole shows very different per-candidate training times (Base 14.4s vs Ours 67.2s); and the large MNIST-1D gain (70.25 -> 95.99) is reported without protocol-parity details, making it hard to attribute to the editing mechanism.

Baseline provenance is unclear: it is not stated whether the EP/FS/EoH CLRS numbers in Tables 1 and A.1 are reproduced or taken from prior work, and the 'search-and-transfer' protocol (evolve only on DFS, transfer) differs fundamentally from EvoPrompting's multi-task evolution, confounding the head-to-head comparison.

The Operator/Action factorization is manually defined and specific to the CLRS reference program; the claim that SPARK is 'backbone-agnostic' is asserted rather than demonstrated, and generality beyond this one architecture family is not established.

Full-suite results include large regressions (BFS 99.7 -> 70.6, Floyd-Warshall 48.5 -> 32.9, KMP 19.5 -> 14.9), which undercut the 'improved algorithmic alignment' framing and suggest the transferred architecture is not robust; this is acknowledged but not analyzed.

Presentation is overloaded with newly coined terminology (SPARK, ASR, RC, SAR, 'where-then-how', Function-factor Tokens) and heavy bolding, and there are internal inconsistencies (e.g., motivation-figure numbers, slightly different CLRS reference values across tables), which hinder clear assessment.

strengths: Identifies a plausible and well-motivated failure mode ("functional entanglement") and gives it a clear conceptual framing that connects to why free-form LLM code rewrites are hard to control in multi-round search.

Proposes a concrete, implementable mechanism (factor-scoped region tags, ASR scope selection, RC directive, SAR scoped edit, plus a cheap feasibility pipeline) that is straightforward to describe and reproduce at the operator level.

Evaluation breadth is reasonable: a 10-task CLRS main table, a full 30-task CLRS comparison in the appendix, and five additional non-CLRS benchmarks (MNIST-1D, 20News, CartPole-v1, Mice Protein, BCW).

Includes meaningful ablations (ASR-only vs RC+SAR-only under two LLM editors, plus scope-control baselines in Table A.2 that show region tags alone are insufficient), and an honest limitations section that flags transfer failures (BFS, Floyd–Warshall, KMP) and higher search-time LLM cost.
Reports the full 30-task suite (83.91% mean) rather than hiding it, and the qualitative trend on the subset is at least partially consistent with the full-suite numbers.
weaknesses: The headline "28.1× sample-efficient architecture evolution speedup" is not a valid efficiency measurement. It is obtained by noting that SPARK hits 83.74% at its 57th evaluated candidate and that this already exceeds EvoPrompting's *final* DFS result (68.14%) under a 1600-evaluation budget. A genuine speedup requires reaching a *matched* accuracy threshold, and the accounting also ignores that SPARK issues multiple LLM calls per iteration (ASR/RC/SAR), so "evaluations" are not commensurate across methods. This claim is repeated in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion, making it a central overclaim.

Table 1 presents a "representative 10-task subset" that is in fact favorable. Table A.1 shows SPARK degrades sharply on BFS (99.7→70.6), Floyd–Warshall (48.5→32.9), and KMP (19.5→14.9). Labeling the subset "representative" while excluding the tasks where the method fails materially misrepresents the method's reliability.

The claim that gains are "not explained by capacity/compute scaling" rests only on MACs. The evolved program (Listing 6) clearly adds multiple new layers (aggr_mixer, res_gate, gate_node, gate_edge, gate_global, extra heads), and parameter count—which Section 3.1 says is part of the descriptor φ—is never reported in Table 1. Without parameter counts, the capacity-neutrality claim is unsupported.

Budget accounting across baselines is inconsistent: OpenEvolve/FunSearch are run at 100 attempts, EvoPrompting is quoted at 1600 evaluations, and the speedup metric then mixes these two regimes. This undermines the controlled-comparison framing in Section 4.

Architecture search is performed only on CLRS dfs; all other CLRS tasks are pure transfer ("without task-specific evolution"), while EvoPrompting evolves per-task. The entire search-operator contribution therefore rests on a single task, and the cross-task table mixes transfer with per-task evolution.

No variance or error bars are reported on the main results despite the abstract/intro stating results are reported over multiple seeds; only Fig. A.1 shows 5-seed bands for dynamics. Several non-CLRS differences are within plausible noise (Mice Protein 61.78 vs 61.78; BCW 96.90 vs 97.04; 20News 59.13 vs 58.05), so the generalization claim from Table 2 is weak.

Fig. 2's entanglement-rate and valid-rate comparisons are partly circular—SPARK is explicitly designed to restrict edits to one region, so a lower entanglement rate is expected by construction. The valid rate still stabilizes at only ~0.5–0.6, meaning roughly half of proposals remain invalid even under SPARK, which weakens the reliability narrative.

The OPERATOR/ACTION factorization is manually defined and CLRS-specific (acknowledged as a limitation). Generality is asserted from modest non-CLRS gains that rely on the same manual region-tagging machinery, so it is unclear how the method transfers without hand-defined factors.

Reproducibility is limited: the editor is a proprietary/black-box API model (DeepSeek-R1-0528) with fixed temperature 0.7, main-table numbers appear to come from a single run, and no variance is given, making it difficult for others to verify the magnitude of the reported gains.

strengths: Clearly identifies and operationalizes a concrete, plausible failure mode—functional entanglement—with an explicit definition (non-factor-local diffs touching multiple functional regions or frozen scaffolding) and ties it to executability and search dynamics.

The factor-conditioned editing primitive (ASR scope selection → RC directive → SAR scoped edit) is a sensible, well-motivated decomposition, and the paper correctly frames 'where-then-how' as the key mechanism rather than refinement alone.

Ablation evidence directly supports the central claim: Table 3 (ASR vs RC+SAR vs full SPARK) across two editors (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-Plus) shows scope selection matters most, and Table A.2 isolates region-tag-only, random-scope, fixed-scope, and no-RC variants, showing gains come from the full pipeline rather than tagging alone.

Evaluation spans the representative 10-task subset plus the full 30-task CLRS suite to reduce task-selection bias, and adds five non-CLRS benchmarks (MNIST-1D, 20News, CartPole-v1, Mice Protein, BCW) to test transferability of the mechanism.
The paper reports MACs alongside accuracy to argue that gains are not from capacity scaling, and Fig. A.1 tracks best-so-far MACs to support this over the search trajectory.
The limitations section is honest, acknowledging uneven task transfer, added LLM-call cost, and the manually defined two-factor design.
weaknesses: The headline '28.1× sample-efficient speedup' is not a controlled comparison: it divides EvoPrompting's 1600-evaluation budget by SPARK's 57 evaluated candidates, while the paper itself states EP evolves across multiple tasks and SPARK evolves only on dfs then transfers. This cross-paper, non-equivalent accounting should not be a primary quantitative claim.

Baseline protocols in Table 1 are inconsistent: EP numbers are taken from its paper (multi-task evolution) while OE/FS/EoH are re-run under a dfs-only evolution setting. Mixing these makes the per-task comparisons difficult to interpret and may inflate SPARK's apparent margins.

Main results (Table 1) report single point estimates with no seeds or error bars, despite the text claiming results over multiple random seeds; the only multi-seed evidence (Fig. A.1) covers search progress, not final accuracies, leaving the significance of the reported gains unclear.

Some reported numbers appear internally inconsistent and suggest reporting/reproducibility problems: e.g., in Table A.5 for Breast Cancer Wisconsin, OE/EP show substantially higher accuracy (96.90) than Base (95.13) yet far worse loss (0.97 vs 0.13); Table A.4 MNIST-1D shows Ours MLP at 88.36% accuracy with loss 0.99 while Base MLP is 64.0% with loss 3.01. These patterns are not explained and undermine confidence in the numbers.

Search-time overhead is understated: Table A.5 shows per-candidate training time for Ours on CartPole-v1 at 67.18s vs 19.01s for OE (~3.5×), and SPARK issues multiple LLM calls per proposal (ASR/RC/SAR). Framing this only as 'additional LLM calls' while emphasizing comparable MACs underplays the real search cost.

Transfer regressions are large and only briefly noted: on the full 30-task suite SPARK drops sharply on BFS (99.7→70.6), Floyd–Warshall (48.5→32.9), KMP (19.5→14.9), MCO, and MKr, which weakens the generalization narrative and suggests the evolved dfs architecture is not broadly transferable.

Reproducibility is limited: prompts, exact region/boundary-tag definitions, and feasibility-check specifications are only partially described, the LLM is a non-deterministic black-box API (DeepSeek-R1-0528), and the code URL is truncated in the provided text.

Originality is modest: scope-constrained/AST- or region-restricted editing and structure-aware mutation operators are well-established, so the contribution is largely a targeted re-combination for the LLM-NAS setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The causal story linking entanglement → executability → progress is presented largely as correlational curves (Fig. 2); the paper offers a simple p_e^k heuristic but no direct intervention isolating entanglement from other confounds.
